preamble: A nasalized front mid vowel lowers to the open nasal [ã] and merges with it. Nasality blurs vowel-height contrasts, so mid nasal vowels tend to lower. In Old French, [ẽ] from Latin e before a nasal consonant lowered and merged with [ã] in the 11th to early 12th century, which is why en and an sound alike today (dent and dans both have [ɑ̃]). Anglo-Norman did not share the change. In the Lechitic branch of West Slavic, the Proto-Slavic front nasal *ę lost its front quality and merged with the back nasal as [ã]. Old Polish then split this vowel by length into ę and ą, while Kashubian keeps [ã] in words such as jãzëk 'language' and miãso 'meat'.

examples.note: Nasal [ẽ] lowered and merged with the reflex of Latin an during the 11th or early 12th century. Old Norman and Anglo-Norman did not take part. Later [ã] backed to [ɑ̃].
Same merger: vent now has the same vowel as vante, and en/an spellings are pronounced identically.
In Old Polish *ę and *ǫ merged in quality into a single nasal [ã], and the merged vowel kept a length contrast. The short [ã] became modern ę.
The long variant of the merged [ã] became modern ą. This gives the alternation pięć ~ piąty.
The Proto-Slavic front nasal is continued as [ã] (written ã); compare Polish język.
Same reflex *ę > ã; also dzesãc 'ten' from *desętь.
